articles.title: TikTok bans Musk documentary account
articles.summary: Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney's Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film's social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
body: Larry Ellison’s TikTok has shut down the promotional account for Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary.
While TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film via a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase.

Banning the documentary’s account, however, marks a serious escalation, and one laced with a dash of irony — shortly before the account was removed, it posted that people should see the movie “before it gets shut down.”

articles.title: Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and scary – Chinese AI
articles.summary: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China. There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge.
body: Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.
In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by.

The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries.
It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again.
points: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China.
There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge.
In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by.
The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point.

articles.title: SpaceX’s ambitious, expensive gamble to replace AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
articles.summary: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.
body: Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”

Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.

I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast.

articles.title: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
articles.summary: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors. “I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.
body: It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.
But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.

One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.
Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.
points: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors.
“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.

articles.title: Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
articles.summary: Earlier this year, Mercedes' AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower.
body: It may even out-muscle the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric and Lucid Gravity.

The AMG GT SUV (say that five times fast) marks the first time in the performance brand’s 59-year history that it has developed a full-size SUV entirely in-house from the ground up. Scheduled to hit the US next summer, the new EV is built on Merc’s high-performance AMG.EA architecture to combine sports-car handling with full-size SUV suburban practicality.

It will be available in three trims — GT 53, GT 55, and the flagship GT 63 — with the top model delivering 1,153hp via the same three axial flux motors powering the four-door coupe. That beats the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric with Launch Control, which is sure to make for some awkward run-ins around Stuttgart.

Thanks to an 800-volt architecture, the SUV supports blistering-fast charging speeds up to 710kW on the 128kWh battery (GT 63 / GT 55) and 600kW on the 106kWh battery (GT 53). Drivers can charge 10–80 percent in 12 minutes or gain up to 450km (around 280 miles) of WLTP range in just 10 minutes. The 128kWh battery trims will have an estimated max range of 435 miles.
points: Earlier this year, Mercedes' AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower.
It may even out-muscle the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric and Lucid Gravity.

articles.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
articles.summary: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time.
body: Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.

Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.
points: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world.
CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings.
Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time.
Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible?

articles.title: Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline
articles.summary: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators. It started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn.
body: I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes.

It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t.

It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing as Caroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it.

Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicine contacted me to ask whether I’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well.
points: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators.

articles.title: Why BioWare's Neverwinter Nights still has thousands of active players
articles.summary: Neverwinter Nights was made by the studio that produced seminal RPGs Baldur's Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect, and Dragon Age. It sold well and was critically acclaimed at launch.
body: Nonetheless, more than two decades later, it still has a tight-knit and surprisingly active community that none of those other games can rival. I think that’s partly because it was a completely different beast.

BioWare is known for making multi-character, story-driven role-playing games that focused primarily on single-player story campaigns, though some supported co-op play in those campaigns. With Neverwinter Nights, BioWare instead made a game that was as focused on a modding toolset for content creation as it was on giving players a pre-packaged story, and that emphasized multiplayer at least as much as solo play.

Today you would expect this to be a calculated attempt to bring more long-term, always-on, multiplayer-as-a-service to an RPG franchise that has mostly appealed to solo players. You might imagine it would be about selling cosmetics, a subscription, or a battle pass, or maybe you would think it was about nabbing appealing engagement numbers.

But it’s clear from playing it today that Neverwinter Nights wasn’t primarily made for those reasons. Instead, it came from a passion for tabletop role-playing and a desire to get closer to that in video game form than ever before.

articles.title: Ministers must be honest about Russian threat to UK, says former Foreign Office head
articles.summary: Peter Ricketts calls for more resilience in protecting banking, energy and water systems from cyber-assaults. Ministers need to be honest with the British public about the immediate threat posed by Russia, which could soon lead to lives being lost, a former national security adviser has said.
body: Peter Ricketts, who advised David Cameron when he was prime minister, became the latest figure to warn about the scale of the threat posed by “hybrid attacks” from Vladimir Putin’s forces.

The peer, who is the former top civil servant in the Foreign Office, said banking systems, energy or water supplies could be targeted by Kremlin cyber-assaults. He called for further investment in resilience for key sectors.
It comes in a week where the heads of MI5 and the British army have warned about the danger posed by Moscow.
Lord Ricketts also dismissed Andy Burnham’s claim he wanted to be a “bridge” between the US and Ukraine.

articles.title: OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, but the body isn't the real challenge
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants a humanoid that can operate in a world designed for people, though the CEO says a robot 'brain' is a much bigger challenge.
body: Figuring out how the 'brain' will work will take a lot of time.
While OpenAI is already busy with the development of AI models and new consumer hardware, CEO Sam Altman and his team apparently have time for one more project: a humanoid robot.

On the Sources podcast, Altman explained that the human form is logical because "the world is very much designed for people." Doors, keyboards and tools are all designed around a certain type of body, and a robot that can move around in the same spaces should probably have a similar form factor. As Altman put it, "matching that form factor seems good."

When asked if OpenAI will actually build one, his response was much more succinct: "We will." However, Altman isn't so concerned with the nitty-gritty details of what that robot looks like. Those questions are "less important than really figuring out... the brain that makes the robot work," he said. Basically, giving a machine two arms and two legs doesn't get you very far if it doesn't know what to do with them.
points: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants a humanoid that can operate in a world designed for people, though the CEO says a robot 'brain' is a much bigger challenge.
